<reason>Side B won by exposing a fatal contradiction at the heart of Side A's case. Side A argued that existing unit prices are in tiny, inconsistent print or hidden behind app taps, yet claimed an asymmetric warning on a downsized product would not mislead shoppers into buying a costlier rival because shoppers would compare the two products' unit prices. As Side B pointed out, because the mandate only triggers on downsized packages, the rival's unit price remains buried in fine print or behind a tap, leaving only a glaring penalty badge on the cheaper option. Side B also won the operational clash after Side A dropped the rebuttal that app customers order before workers pick from mixed transitional shelf stock.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In [B4.2]-[B4.3] and [B5.2]-[B5.3], Side B turned Side A's own premise against its mechanism: if baseline unit prices are unreadably small, mismatched, or hidden behind app taps, a shopper cannot compare a flagged product's £1.11/100g against an unflagged rival's £1.25/100g, because the mandate leaves the rival's unit price untouched and unread.</best_rebuttal>
